facts.fact: The World Bank diagnostic, from interviews of 12 to 22 January 2017, states that civil registration records are paper based, that acts are registered and archived locally at the primary centres with no central register or archive, and that at the Niamey 4th arrondissement office the process and archives are wholly paper-based, on typewriters and by hand.

The World Bank diagnostic (field work January 2017) describes births, deaths and marriages as recorded in paper notification books and paper registers kept in three copies, and states there is no centralised database for civil registration.

The World Bank diagnostic (field work January 2017) reports no office entering events digitally: records are paper based and held at municipal level; the Ministry of Interior counted 16,093 civil registration offices in 2016, of which 10,848 were operational.

The World Bank diagnostic states that the civil registration system is governed by the Ministry of Interior, through its directorate general for refugees and civil status, with mayors heading the registry in each commune (field work January 2017).

The World Bank diagnostic states that the civil registration service is funded by state budget allocations to the communes, of an amount the legal framework does not specify, and that in January 2017 registrars at a Niamey primary centre had gone seven months unpaid.
